issues.title: [Feature] Docs: Add a guide for Delivering Remote Images
issues.body:
# **Feature Request**

## **Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

Delivering Remote Images should describe two ways to handle remote images including the fetch API via:
```
deliveryType="fetch"
```

And using auto-upload via URL mapping

How: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LJhsn5A0PFE

issues.title: Improvements to "Building App Forms" page
issues.body:
I think the ["Building App Forms"](https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/apps/tutorials/app-forms/) page could use some improvements:

* LibreOffice won (in my and [other's](https://hackaday.com/2020/11/02/openoffice-or-libreoffice-a-star-is-torn/) opinions). We should change:
   > Google sheets or other preferred editor like Excel or Open Office

   to:

   > [Google Sheets](https://www.google.com/sheets/about/) or other preferred editor like [Excel](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/excel) or [LibreOffice](https://www.libreoffice.org/)
* The step one of ["Define XLS Survey/Form Fields"](https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/apps/tutorials/app-forms/#1-define-xls-surveyform-fields) is laborious and error prone to copy to a local spreadsheet.  We should offer either an easier copy and paste-able content or a `.xlsx` to download (and include  "choices" and "settings" worksheets too). This applies to other instances where we inline the content of a spreadsheet , like [tasks](https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/apps/tutorials/tasks/).
* In the "Next Steps" section at the bottom of the page, it wasn't immediately clear that I should go to the [Setting Form Properties](https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/apps/tutorials/form-properties/) page.  We should add an explicit, easy to click link!

## Good first issue

This ticket has the [Good first issue label](https://github.com/medic/cht-core/issues?q=state%3Aopen%20label%3A%22Good%20first%20issue%22)! This means it’s been especially curated by other CHT contributors to be easy to work on for first time contributors per [the docs](https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/community/contributing/creating-good-first-issues/).

To succeed on this ticket, please:

1. remove mention of open office and mention LibreOffice 
2. Add links to Excel and LibreOffice home pages
3. For the "Define XLS Survey/Form Fields" section, either create a `assessment.xlsx`  file for easy download, or experiment with markdown content that reliably copy an pastes into a spreadhseet well.
4. Add  link in the "Next section" to [Setting Form Properties](https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/apps/tutorials/form-properties/)  replacing the unlinked text

issues.title: STY: Enforce Ruff rule B905, zip-without-explicit-strict
issues.body:
`zip` calls should ideally specify `strict=True` since most of the time there's an underlying assumption that the input arguments are of equal length. To enforce this we should enable the Ruff rule zip-without-explicit-strict, https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/zip-without-explicit-strict/

Since there are about ~500 occurrences of `zip` in the code base, this issue should be completed in multiple PRs that adds `strict=True` to `zip` calls in a particular directory. Therefore, this issue can be worked on by multiple contributors.

For those interested in working on this issue:

1. Comment below on which directory you'll be working on. If you want to work on `pandas/core`, please choose a subdirectory in this location e.g. `pandas/core/internals`
2. Submit a PR adding `strict=True` (or `strict=False` if necessary) to `zip` calls

Once all `zip` calls are have a `strict` argument, a separate PR will be needed to move `"B905"` from the ignore section to the select section. https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/98c9c7f838d223e66f1459fab23ac178b29c2227/pyproject.toml#L395

issues.title: Optimise the `get_spectrogram` method
issues.body:
## Description
<!-- Provide a clear and concise description of the new feature you'd like -->
The [`get_spectrogram`](https://github.com/jcfitzpatrick12/spectre-core/blob/v1.2.0/src/spectre_core/batches/_batches.py#L164-L198) method currently retrieves spectrograms for a specified time interval by opening every fits file and checking if its time range overlaps with the requested interval. This is inefficient, as files that are clearly outside the interval are still read and processed, leading to unnecessary I/O and slower performance.

The root cause is that the file name only encodes the spectrogram's start time, while the end time can only be determined by inspecting the file contents. To improve this, we can use the start time of the next spectrogram file to upper bound the end time of the previous one, allowing us to filter out irrelevant files without opening them. This change would significantly reduce the number of files that need to be read. 

This is a real bottleneck on the Raspberry Pi - so a helpful one to tackle.

issues.title: Restructure the docs of Readme and Contribution
issues.body:
##  Issue: Restructure Documentation & Update Contribution Guide

### Description

We need to restructure our documentation for better clarity and consistency. Currently, `README.md` and `Contribution.md` are in the root directory, but we want to follow a cleaner structure by moving all documentation-related files into a `docs/` folder.

Additionally, In future we need to update the contribution guide to reflect the **three database environments** we use:

1. **Local Development** → PostgreSQL running via Docker container
2. **Staging** → Neon database instance
3. **Production** → GCP-managed PostgreSQL

The contribution guide should include clear steps for running **Postgres in Docker for local development**.

---

### Tasks

* [ ] Move `Contribution.md` and related documentation (`README.md`, etc.) into a `docs/` folder.
* [ ] Update references/links to reflect the new location.
* [ ] Update `Contribution.md` with new database setup details.

  * Add a section explaining the Local environment in Docker
  * Provide instructions to spin up a local Postgres container using Docker.

---

###  Example: Local PostgreSQL Setup via Docker

```bash
# Pull Postgres Docker image
docker pull postgres:15

# Run Postgres container
docker run --name sst-dashboard-db \
  -e POSTGRES_USER=admin \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=admin \
  -e POSTGRES_DB=sst_dashboard \
  -p 5432:5432 \
  -d postgres:15


```

Add the following to your `.env.local`:

```env
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://admin:admin@localhost:5432/sst_dashboard
```

---

###  Required Folder Structure

```
dashboard/
├── docs/
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── Contribution.md
│   └── other-docs.md
└── ...
```

---

###  Expected Outcome

* Cleaner project structure with centralised documentation inside `docs/`.
* Updated contribution guide that clearly outlines how to set up database in local environment.
* Local devs can quickly get started using Dockerized Postgres without manual setup.

issues.title: Deprecate `generate_signature_output` in favor of input_example
issues.body:
### Summary

The [mlflow.transformers.generate_signature_output](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/python_api/mlflow.transformers.html#mlflow.transformers.generate_signature_output) function is an utility function for generating prediction output for a Transformers model, so that users can pass it to the `mlflow.models.infer_signature` for getting the auto-inferred model signature for the model.

However, MLflow now support inferring signature from `input_example` specified when logging a model. Users no longer need this API and can just pass an input example to let MLflow infer the signature.

We should mark the `generate_signature_output` deprecated, as well as update the examples and tutorials in the documentation.

**Old**
```
signature = mlflow.models.infer_signature(
    input_example,
    mlflow.transformers.generate_signature_output(generation_pipeline, input_example),
    parameters,
)

with mlflow.start_run() as run:
    model_info = mlflow.transformers.log_model(
        transformers_model=generation_pipeline,
        artifact_path="text_generator",
        input_example=["prompt 1", "prompt 2", "prompt 3"],
        signature=signature,
    )
```

**Current**
```
with mlflow.start_run() as run:
    model_info = mlflow.transformers.log_model(
        transformers_model=generation_pipeline,
        artifact_path="text_generator",
        # By passing a tuple of input example and parameters, MLflow can infer model signature including parameters.
        input_example=(["prompt 1", "prompt 2", "prompt 3"], parameters)
    )
```



### Notes

- Make sure to open a PR from a **non-master** branch.
- Sign off the commit using the `-s` flag when making a commit:

  ```sh
  git commit -s -m "..."
           # ^^ make sure to use this
  ```

- Include `#{issue_number}` (e.g. `#123`) in the PR description when opening a PR.

issues.title: 📊 Tracking Issue: Structured Quantum Programs
issues.body:
This issue tracks the effort to extend [MQT Bench](https://github.com/munich-quantum-toolkit/bench) with support for **structured quantum programs**.  

By *structured quantum programs* we mean **hybrid quantum–classical programs** that go beyond straight-line circuits and include:  
- Structured control flow operations (`if`, `for`, `while`, etc.)  
- Dynamic quantum circuit primitives (mid-circuit measurements, resets, classically controlled quantum gates)  

The goal of this roadmap is to provide an **overview of the different available kinds of structured programs** and to act as a **tracking hub** for adding them to the MQT Bench suite.  

👉 **Contributions are highly encouraged!** Even adding a single primitive or algorithm is already a great start. Please see our [contribution guidelines](https://mqt.readthedocs.io/projects/bench/en/latest/contributing.html) before getting started.  
👉 **Important:** Checkboxes should only be marked once the corresponding PR has been merged.  

These benchmarks are expected to serve not only as **functional tests** but also as **challenges for compilers, visualization engines, runtimes, and emulators**, since they combine quantum and classical control in nontrivial ways.

---

## 🔁 Loops and Iteration

Loops are a fundamental control-flow construct. They can appear with **static bounds** (fixed iteration counts) or **dynamic bounds** (e.g., repeat-until-success). Many important algorithms can be expressed naturally in this form.

- [ ] **Static loops**  
  - Example: **Grover’s Algorithm** (repeated oracle + diffusion steps)  
    *Ref:* [Grover, 1996](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9605043)  
  - Example: **GHZ state preparation** (iterative entangling gates)  
  - Example: **Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT)** (nested controlled rotations)  
  - Example: **Iterative Phase Estimation (iQPE)** (looped controlled unitaries)  
    *Ref:* [Iterative QPE](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0610214)  

- [ ] **Dynamic loops (Repeat-Until-Success)**  
  - Example: **Quantum Metropolis Sampling**  
    *Ref:* [Temme et al., 2011](https://arxiv.org/abs/0911.3635)  
  - Example: **ML-QAE (Quantum Amplitude Estimation)**  
    *Ref:* [Suzuki et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.10246)  
  - Example: **X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy (XAS)** (loop structure with likely static bounds)  
    *Ref:* [Quantum simulation of XAS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.11015)  

---

## 🧱 Block Encoding

Block encoding embeds classical data or operators into quantum states. It underpins advanced algorithms like QSVT.

- [ ] **Block encoding primitive**  
  *Ref:* [Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.01838)  
  - Example: **QSVT / QSP**  
    *Ref:* [Low & Chuang, 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.02685)  

---

## ✨ Teleportation

Quantum teleportation is a canonical primitive for quantum communication and distributed computing.

- [ ] **Teleportation primitive**  
  *Ref:* [Bennett et al., 1993](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.70.1895)  
  - Example: **Teleportation-based subroutines** (used in distributed algorithms, fault-tolerant protocols)  

---

## 🎛 Multiplexers

Quantum multiplexers allow conditional application of gates and are widely used in circuit synthesis and algorithm design.

- [ ] **Multiplexer primitive**  
  *Ref:* [Quantum multiplexers in circuit synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0410066)  
  - Example: **Grover’s Algorithm** (oracle construction often uses multiplexed operations)  

---

## 🔄 Dynamic Qubit (Re)-Allocation

Dynamic allocation and reuse of qubits is crucial for resource-efficient algorithms. This often involves mid-circuit measurement and reset.

- [ ] **Dynamic qubit allocation primitive**  
  - Example: **Iterative Phase Estimation (iQPE)**  
  - Example: **Iterative QFT**  
  - Example: **Shor’s Algorithm**  
    *Ref:* [Shor, 1994](https://doi.org/10.1137/S0097539795293172)  

---

## ⚛️ Loosely Coupled Hybrid Programs

Variational and hybrid algorithms naturally combine quantum circuits with classical optimization loops. They are *loosely coupled* because the quantum and classical parts interact only at well-defined synchronization points.

- [ ] **VQE (Variational Quantum Eigensolver)**  
  *Ref:* [Peruzzo et al., 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1304.3061)  

- [ ] **QAOA (Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm)**  
  *Ref:* [Farhi et al., 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.4028)  

---

## 🧩 Fault-Tolerance & Resource States

Structured programs also include primitives for error correction and fault-tolerant computation.

- [ ] **Magic State Distillation**  
  *Ref:* [Bravyi & Kitaev, 2005](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0403025)

issues.title: [asan] NPD calling prctl with PR_SET_VMA PR_SET_VMA_ANON_NAME and nullptr for name
issues.body:
```c++
unsigned long name = reinterpret_cast<unsigned long>(nullptr);
prctl(PR_SET_VMA, PR_SET_VMA_ANON_NAME, start, len, name);
```
will crash in `internal_strlen` called from the prctl asan interceptor.

`man 2 prctl` states:

> PR_SET_VMA (since Linux 5.17)
> PR_SET_VMA_ANON_NAME
> If arg5  is  NULL, the name of the appropriate anonymous virtual memory areas will be re‐set.

So it is valid and expected to be able to call `prctl` with the 5th parameter set to `NULL`.  It's UB to call `strlen` with `NULL`; and in this case, `internal_strlen` immediately dereferences the pointer it's given.

a4c97e1937997

cc @vitalybuka @eugenis @devnexen

issues.title: APIs and Microservices in a Hybrid System: Architecture, Challenges, and Strategy
issues.body:
APIs and Microservices in a Hybrid System: Architecture, Challenges, and Strategy
Executive Summary
The interconnected nature of modern digital services is built upon a foundation of Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) and microservices. When deployed in a hybrid cloud environment—which blends public cloud, private cloud, and on-premises data centers—this architectural model becomes a powerful strategic tool for businesses. APIs function as the "digital glue" that allows disparate software components to communicate, while a microservices architecture breaks down monolithic applications into smaller, independent, and highly manageable services. This report will provide a comprehensive analysis of the role of APIs and microservices in a hybrid system, detailing the architectural patterns, the critical challenges, and the profound strategic benefits that this approach can deliver.
1. The Foundation: Microservices and the Hybrid Cloud
A hybrid microservices architecture is a sophisticated approach that combines two distinct but highly complementary concepts: the microservices design pattern and a hybrid cloud infrastructure. Understanding each component is essential to grasping the full power and complexity of the combined model.
1.1. Defining Microservices Architecture
Microservices represent an architectural approach where an application is broken down into a collection of small, independent services. Unlike a traditional monolithic system, which uses a single, interdependent codebase to perform multiple business functions, each microservice is designed to perform a single, specialized task. These services are "loosely coupled," meaning they can be developed, deployed, and maintained independently without affecting the others. The communication between these services is standardized through a well-defined interface, which is the API.
1.2. The Hybrid Cloud Environment
A hybrid cloud is a blended computing environment that utilizes a mix of resources from public clouds, private clouds, and on-premises data centers. This model is gaining significant traction because it allows organizations to leverage the flexibility and cost-effectiveness of public clouds while maintaining control and security over their private infrastructure. Hybrid cloud management (HCM) software facilitates the seamless integration and orchestration of these diverse environments.
1.3. The Interplay of Microservices and Hybrid Cloud
The combination of these two concepts creates a highly flexible and scalable system. Hybrid multicloud environments are particularly well-suited for supporting microservices, which communicate via APIs. This architecture allows organizations to place workloads in the most suitable environment—for example, running core, latency-sensitive microservices on-premises while using the public cloud's elasticity to handle fluctuating demand for less-critical services.
2. The Role of APIs: The Digital Connective Tissue
In a microservices architecture, APIs are not just communication tools; they are the fundamental "backbone" that enables the entire system to function. They serve as a contract that defines how services will communicate, enabling a range of critical benefits.
 * Decoupling: APIs allow each service to be developed and managed independently. A service only needs to know how to interact with another service's API, not its internal logic or technology stack. This loose coupling means a change in one service does not require changes in others, simplifying maintenance and accelerating development.
 * Interoperability: Since APIs define a standardized communication protocol, they enable microservices built with different programming languages or technologies to work together seamlessly. This allows development teams to choose the best tool for each specific service, enhancing agility and flexibility.
 * Faster Development: By relying on APIs, development teams can work on different services simultaneously without code conflicts or interdependency issues. This parallel development approach shortens development cycles and enables organizations to get new features and applications to market faster.
3. Architecting the Hybrid System: Gateways and Meshes
A well-designed hybrid microservices system requires a layered approach to managing communication, especially the flow of traffic into and between services. This is where API gateways and service meshes play their distinct yet complementary roles.
3.1. The API Gateway: The Front Door
An API gateway is a centralized entry point that sits at the "edge" of the system, acting as a single, stable interface for clients to access backend services. It acts as a reverse proxy, routing incoming requests from external clients to the appropriate microservice. A gateway also provides cross-cutting functionality, offloading critical tasks from individual services, such as:
 * Security: It acts as the first line of defense, handling authentication and authorization (e.g., token-based authentication), rate limiting, and firewalls.
 * Traffic Management: It manages load balancing, caching, and routing requests to the correct services.
 * Aggregation and Transformation: It can combine responses from multiple services into a single, cohesive response for the client, reducing chattiness between the client and backend.
3.2. The Service Mesh: The Internal Network
A service mesh is an infrastructure layer that handles communication between microservices within an application. It uses a "sidecar" proxy for each service instance, which intercepts all inbound and outbound traffic. This abstracts away the complexity of inter-service communication, allowing services to focus on their core business logic. A service mesh provides crucial functions for internal traffic, including:
 * Reliability: It manages traffic, health checks, and observability, such as collecting metrics on latency and error rates.
 * Security: It can enforce security policies and encrypt communication between services using mutual TLS (mTLS).
 * Policy Enforcement: A service mesh provides a centralized configuration for enforcing service policies like quotas and authentication.
3.3. API Gateways and Service Meshes Together
In a hybrid system, API gateways and service meshes work in tandem. The API gateway manages north-south traffic (external client-to-service communication), while the service mesh handles east-west traffic (internal service-to-service communication). This combination provides a robust solution where external access is secured and managed by the gateway, and internal communications are secured and made reliable by the mesh.
4. Navigating the Challenges of Hybrid Microservices
While offering significant benefits, a hybrid microservices architecture introduces a new set of challenges that must be carefully managed.
 * Complexity: This architecture is more complex to develop, deploy, and maintain than a monolithic application because it involves multiple codebases and deployment units. Debugging can be particularly challenging as issues need to be traced across numerous, independently running services that may use different programming languages.
 * Security: A distributed system increases the application's attack surface, as each microservice communication point is a potential vulnerability. Hybrid and multi-cloud environments compound this challenge by making it difficult to maintain consistent security policies and data protection strategies across different cloud providers and on-premises infrastructure.
 * Data Consistency: In a microservices model, each service typically manages its own data, which creates a challenge for maintaining data consistency across the entire application. This requires carefully designing systems to handle "eventual consistency" or implementing complex patterns for distributed transactions, which can be difficult to implement correctly.
5. Strategic Benefits and Real-World Applications
Despite the challenges, the strategic benefits of a hybrid microservices architecture are compelling, driving innovation and efficiency across industries.
 * Scalability: The ability to scale services independently is a core advantage. During peak demand, only the services experiencing high traffic need to be scaled up, optimizing resource usage and keeping costs in check. In a hybrid cloud, this means a business can use the public cloud's elasticity for bursty workloads, ensuring high performance without over-provisioning resources on-premises.
 * Flexibility and Agility: The loosely coupled nature of microservices allows teams to rapidly develop and deploy new features, accelerating time-to-market. If a business wants to replace a component or integrate a new technology, it can do so for a single service without disrupting the entire system.
 * Modernization and Innovation: This architecture is a key strategy for modernizing legacy monolithic applications, allowing a business to incrementally break down a large, rigid codebase into smaller, more manageable services. This approach is fundamental to cloud-native development and is being leveraged by companies to become more agile, efficient, and responsive to customer needs.

issues.title: [Improvement] Fix concurrancy issues in AuthorizationRequestContext.java loadRole

### What would you like to be improved?

In core/src/main/java/org/apache/gravitino/authorization/AuthorizationRequestContext.java, the loadRole method has a concurrency issue.

The current implementation checks the hasLoadRole flag before invoking the initializer, but it only set the flag to true after the runnable finished. Two threads racing through this code could both see hasLoadRole.get() as false, execute runnable.run(), and only then store true, so the initializer might run twice or more in parallel.

app.add_route("/metrics", make_asgi_app())
```

with:

```
app.mount("/metrics", make_asgi_app())
```

This will correctly expose the ASGI metrics app at /metrics.

issues.title: ENH: Change ExtensionOpsMixin behaviour to not add new operator method if one is already defined on the ExtensionArray class
issues.body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [X] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

ExtensionScalarOpsMixin is convenient for automatically adding arithmetic and comparison operator support to custom Extension Type ExtensionArrays, using scalar type implementations.

However, performing element-wise operations is very inefficient so it is often desirable to implement custom operator or comparison methods on the ExtensionArray class which could use vectorised approaches for much improved performance.

Currently, `MyExtensionArray._add_arithmetic_ops()` and `MyExtensionArray._add_comparison_ops()` overrides any existing defined operator overload methods on `MyExtensionArray`, so if a developer wishes to define any custom operator implementation for enhanced performance, they must abandon `ExtensionScalarOpsMixin` entirely and define ALL arithmetic and comparison operators themselves (not possible to have combination of manually defined operators and element-wise implementation fallback for the others)



### Feature Description

I think it would be very useful for the `_add_*_ops()` methods of `ExtensionOpsMixin` to first check if each operator overload method is already defined on the class before adding it. This would allow the developer to define some particular custom operator methods on the custom ExtensionArray for enhanced performance, but with fallback to the element-wise implementation from ExtensionScalarOpsMixin for those that are not defined. 

An example implementation could like like:

Original:

```
    @classmethod
    def _add_comparison_ops(cls) -> None:
        setattr(cls, "__eq__", cls._create_comparison_method(operator.eq))
        setattr(cls, "__ne__", cls._create_comparison_method(operator.ne))
        setattr(cls, "__lt__", cls._create_comparison_method(operator.lt))
        setattr(cls, "__gt__", cls._create_comparison_method(operator.gt))
        setattr(cls, "__le__", cls._create_comparison_method(operator.le))
        setattr(cls, "__ge__", cls._create_comparison_method(operator.ge))
```

New:
```
    @classmethod
    def _add_comparison_ops(cls) -> None:
        for name, op in [
              ("__eq__", operator.eq),
              ("__ne__", operator.ne),
              ("__lt__", operator.lt),
              ("__gt__", operator.gt),
              ("__le__", operator.le),
              ("__ge__", operator.ge)]:
              if not hasattr(cls, name):
                    setattr(cls, name cls._create_comparison_method(op))
```

This check could also potentially be controlled by  an optional flag argument to `_add_*_ops()` methods to maintain backwards compatible behaviour if desired.

### Alternative Solutions

None that I know of

### Additional Context

_No response_

### 🎨 Enhancement: Show Username on Activity Cards

**Summary**  
Currently, when someone highlights text and votes on it, the resulting activity card displays only the user’s avatar. To improve clarity and attribution, the user’s **username** should also appear next to their avatar, above the timestamp.

- [ ] Username is positioned to the right of the avatar and above the timestamp.  
- [ ] Layout is compatible on desktop and mobile.  
- [ ] UI does not truncate or overlap long usernames.  

---

**Tech Notes**  
- Ensure GraphQL/REST query for activity feed includes `username` along with `avatar` and `timestamp`.  
- Update the Activity Card component to render `username`.  
- Align styles with existing text styles for activity metadata.  

---

**Priority**  
Medium – Improves transparency and usability in activity feeds, but not mission critical.

issues.title: OPTIONS calls are not exempt from authentication for API resources defined in `deployment.toml`.
issues.body:
### Current Limitation

$subject

1. Add the following/similar config to deployment.toml

[[resource.access_control]]
context = "(.*)/scim2/Agents(.*)"
secure="true"
http_method="all"

2. Observe that OPTIONS requests to the specified context are also being treated as secured, even though the OPTIONS requests are explicitly marked as not secured in https://github.com/wso2/carbon-identity-framework/blob/7a963796deed02100f76dd80c132228de91346a8/features/identity-core/org.wso2.carbon.identity.core.server.feature/resources/resource-access-control-v2.xml.j2#L44

So, Ideally the OPTIONS calls should not be treated as secured, but they are being treated so for api resources defined as mentioned in step 01 in deployment.toml.

Move https://github.com/wso2/carbon-identity-framework/blob/master/features/identity-core/org.wso2.carbon.identity.core.server.feature/resources/resource-access-control-v2.xml.j2#L21-L41 below the configuration for OPTIONS requests.

issues.title: [Desktop] Allow users to add site exceptions for data that is cleared "on exit"
issues.body:
<!-- Have you searched for similar issues? Before submitting this issue, please check the open issues and add a note before logging a new issue. 

PLEASE USE THE TEMPLATE BELOW TO PROVIDE INFORMATION ABOUT THE ISSUE. 
INSUFFICIENT INFO WILL GET THE ISSUE CLOSED. IT WILL ONLY BE REOPENED AFTER SUFFICIENT INFO IS PROVIDED-->

## Description 
<!--Provide a brief description of the issue-->
As it is now, any data type that is checked in the `Clear browsing data --> [On exit]` will have _all data_ of that type removed upon closing the browser. While this is the intended function, we should implement a function similar to what Microsoft Edge does, where site exceptions can be added to a "Do not clear" list. Data on this list is ignored when the browser runs "clear on exit":

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3299098/85903585-82d53680-b7bb-11ea-8677-61d71c6d3792.png)

This would help users maintain login data for sites they regularly visit and not have to re-authenticate every time data is erased. Additionally, this helps with support, since clearing browsing data often resolves issues with bad cache data -- having the ability to suggest users do this, but without sacrificing specific data they know they want would be very useful and appreciated by users


## Miscellaneous Information:
<!--Any additional information, related issues, extra QA steps, configuration or data that might be necessary to reproduce the issue-->
Original thread that bought this to my attention (again):
https://community.brave.com/t/delete-all-cookies-on-exit-except-allowed-list/137872/5

Users can edit the assigned agent of a meeting even after the meeting has started or ended. Post-meeting edits to the agent should not be allowed.

## 🔄 Steps to Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Go to a completed/ongoing meeting's detail view
2. Click on “Edit”.

- The “Edit” action for Agent should be disabled or hidden for ended meetings.
- Attempts to update the agent via API for ended meetings should be rejected with a clear error (e.g., 400/403) and a user-facing message.

- **OS**: All OS

- **Node.js Version**: Irrelevant
- **pnpm Version**: Irrelevant

### Frontend

- Show tooltip or helper text: “Agent cannot be changed after the meeting has ended/started.”

### Backend

- Enforce immutability rule in the update endpoint: reject agent changes when meeting is ended.
- Return a descriptive error code/message.

issues.title: 🚀 Feature: Central Logging System for Serverless Performance
issues.body:
Build a **custom central logging system** optimized for **performance and cost**, especially suitable for **serverless environments** where cold-start time and execution latency are critical.

---

### ✅ Goal:

Design a **non-blocking, high-performance logging system** that sends application logs asynchronously to **Grafana Loki Cloud**, without slowing down the main application logic.

---

### 💡 Feature Overview:

* Logs should be sent asynchronously through a **lightweight buffered channel** to a central logging handler via Go routines.
* The **central handler** forward logs via **HTTP POST requests** to **Grafana Loki Cloud**.
* Logging should be **completely non-blocking** — the main application **must not wait** for logging operations to complete.
* The system should minimize resource usage and ensure **low-latency**, **cost-efficient** log processing.

---

### 🧪 Performance Notes:

* Serverless functions have **limited runtime (cold start)** and **ephemeral environments**.
* This system **must prioritize** application throughput, not log delivery reliability.
* Logs can be buffered and optionally dropped if system is under pressure (tunable policy).

---

### 🛠️ Tech Stack:

* Logging target: **Grafana Loki Cloud**
* Environment: Optimized for **AWS Lambda / GCP Cloud Functions / etc.**

issues.title: Improve our test coverage
issues.body:
### Feature description

Many of our existing algorithm files have little to no unit testing. This is problematic because this can easily let bugs slip through. We want some assurance that the code we currently have is correct and functional. We welcome all contributors to open PRs to help us add tests to our codebase.

### How to find low-coverage files

Go to the Actions tab in this repository and find the most recent **build** workflow run. Open the logs under "Run Tests" and scroll down until you find the section on code coverage:
```
---------- coverage: platform linux, python 3.12.0-final-0 -----------
Name                                                                          Stmts   Miss  Cover   Missing
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
quantum/q_fourier_transform.py                                                   30     30     0%   14-93
scripts/validate_solutions.py                                                    54     54     0%   2-94
strings/min_cost_string_conversion.py                                            78     75     4%   20-57, 61-75, 79-129
...
```
The "Cover" column tells you what percentage of the lines in that file are covered by tests. We want to increase this percentage for existing files. Find a file with low coverage percentage that you wish to write tests for, add doctests for each function, and open a PR with your changes. You do not need to have a perfect coverage percentage, but all functions should have doctests.

Some files will naturally be hard to write tests for. For example, the file may be poorly written because they lack any functions. Other files might be how-tos, meaning they simply demonstrate how to use an existing library's functions rather than implementing the algorithm themselves. Ignore these kinds of files, as they will need to be rewritten eventually. Furthermore, ignore files in the `web_programming` and `project_euler` directories. Web programming files are inherently hard to test and Project Euler files have their own validation workflow, so don't worry about their test coverage.

_**When you open your PR, put "Contributes to #9943" in the PR description.**_ Do not use the word "fixes", "resolves", or "closes". This issue is an ongoing one, and your PR will not single-handedly resolve this issue.

### How to add doctests

A doctest is a unit test that is contained within the documentation comment (docstring) for a function. Here is an example of what doctests look like within a docstring:
```py
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """
    Adds two non-negative numbers.
    >>> add(1, 1)
    2
    >>> add(2, 5)
    7
    >>> add(1, 0)
    1
    >>> add(-1, -1)
    Traceback (most recent last):
    ...
    ValueError: Numbers must be non-negative
    """
```
For every function in the file you choose, you should write doctests like the ones shown above in its docstring. If a function doesn't have a docstring, add one. Your doctests should be comprehensive but not excessive: you should write just enough tests to cover all basic cases as well as all edge cases (e.g., negative numbers, empty lists, etc).

Do not simply run a function on some example inputs and put its output as the expected output for a doctest. This assumes that the function is implemented correctly when it might not be. Verify independently that your doctests and their expected outputs are correct. **Your PR will not be merged if it has failing tests.** If you happen to discover a bug while writing doctests, please fix it.

_**Please read our [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/TheAlgorithms/Python/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md) before you contribute.**_

issues.title: Guide: Running pytest Before Pull Requests
issues.body:
## Running pytest Before Pull Requests - A Beginner's Guide

This guide explains how to run tests locally before creating a pull request to ensure your code changes work correctly.

### What is pytest?
**pytest** is a Python testing framework that automatically finds and runs test files in your project. It helps verify that your code works as expected and catches errors before they reach the main codebase.

### What is a Virtual Environment?
A **virtual environment** is an isolated Python workspace that keeps your project's dependencies (packages/libraries) separate from other projects. Think of it like a sandbox - changes you make inside won't affect other Python projects on your computer.

---

## Step-by-Step Instructions

### 1. Open Terminal/Command Prompt
Navigate to your project folder:
```powershell
cd C:\Users\[YourUsername]\MyProjects\GitHub\pypdfcodebook
```

### 2. Create a Virtual Environment (First Time Only)
```powershell
python -m venv .venv
```
**What this does:** Creates a new folder called `.venv` containing an isolated Python environment for this project.

### 3. Activate the Virtual Environment
```powershell
.venv\Scripts\Activate
```
**What this does:** "Switches" your terminal to use the isolated Python environment instead of your system's Python.

**How to tell it worked:** Your terminal prompt should now show `(.venv)` at the beginning.

### 4. Install Project Dependencies
Since this project uses modern Python packaging with `pyproject.toml`, install dependencies with:
```powershell
pip install -e .
```
**What this does:** 
- `-e` means "editable install" - installs your project in development mode
- The `.` means "install the current directory as a package"
- This automatically installs all dependencies listed in `pyproject.toml`

### 5. Install Testing Dependencies
```powershell
pip install pytest
```
**What this does:** Installs the pytest testing framework so you can run tests.

### 6. Run the Tests
```powershell
pytest
```
**What this does:** 
- Automatically finds all test files (files starting with `test_` or ending with `_test.py`)
- Runs all the test functions
- Shows you which tests passed ✅ or failed ❌

### 7. Review Test Results
- **Green dots/checkmarks:** Tests passed - your code is working correctly
- **Red F's or error messages:** Tests failed - you need to fix something before making a pull request
- **Yellow warnings:** Usually okay, but worth reviewing

---

## When to Run These Steps

### Every Time You Work on the Project:
1. Navigate to project folder
2. Activate virtual environment (Step 3)
3. Run pytest (Step 6)

### Only Once (Initial Setup):
- Steps 2, 4, and 5 (creating venv and installing dependencies)

---

## Troubleshooting

**Problem:** Terminal shows "command not found" or similar error
**Solution:** Make sure Python is installed and added to your system PATH

**Problem:** Tests fail with import errors
**Solution:** Make sure you activated the virtual environment and installed dependencies

**Problem:** `pytest` command not found
**Solution:** Install pytest: `pip install pytest`

---

## Why This Matters

Running tests locally before creating a pull request:
- ✅ Catches errors early (before they break the main codebase)
- ✅ Saves time (no need to wait for CI/CD to tell you about failures)
- ✅ Shows you're following good development practices
- ✅ Makes your pull requests more likely to be accepted quickly

---

*This guide was created to help establish pytest as part of the standard development workflow for this project.*

issues.title: FEAT(bot): Add interactive help system with command discovery
issues.body:
## Description
The Discord bot lacks an interactive help system that allows users to discover available commands and get detailed usage information.

## Tasks
- Implement a dynamic help command that lists all available commands
- Add command-specific help with usage examples and parameters
- Create command categories (verification, onboarding, admin, etc.)
- Add fuzzy command matching for typo correction

## Acceptance Criteria
- `/help` command shows all available commands grouped by category
- `/help command-name` shows detailed usage for specific commands
- Command suggestions for typos (e.g. '/verif' suggests '/verify')
- Help system automatically updates when new commands are added

## Files to modify
- `bot/src/commands/help.ts` (create new)
- `bot/src/index.ts` (register help command)
- `bot/src/utils/commandLoader.ts` (if exists, for dynamic discovery)

## Testing
- Test help command in both dev and prod environments
- Verify command discovery works for all registered commands
- Test fuzzy matching with various typos
- Ensure help updates automatically with new commands

## Difficulty: Intermediate
## Estimated time: 3-5 hours

issues.title: Including link:
issues.body:
"
Docs
/
More
...
/
Stacks — IaC management
Stacks — IaC management
How to manage Infrastructure as Code at Scale Using Plural

ARTICLES IN THIS SECTION:
The goal of Plural Stacks is to provide a scalable framework to manage infrastructure as code like Terraform, Ansible and Pulumi with a kubernetes-friendly, api-driven approach. The core workflow is as follows:

Declaratively define a stack with a type (terraform, ansible, etc), a location in a git repository to source code from, and a cluster on which it will execute
On each commit to the tracked git repository, a run is created which the Plural deployment operator will detect and execute on the targeted cluster
this allows users to fine grain permissions and network location of IaC runs where both are necessary to configure.
Plural will carefully execute the run for you, and besides basic information like communicating stdout to the UI, we will also gather and present useful information like inputs/outputs, terraform state diagrams and more
On PRs to the tracked repository, a "plan" run is also executed and comments posted on the relevant PR where possible.
To get a better idea of the full power of the experience, feel free to take a look at this demo video (at 2x speed if you want to save some time):


A Basic Stack
The most common way to instantiate a stack is via Kubernetes CRD. This gives a flexible, modular way of recreating infrastructure with Terraform and pairs nicely with our PR Automation tooling for full self-service around IaC.

Here's an example:

YAML
apiVersion: deployments.plural.sh/v1alpha1
kind: InfrastructureStack
metadata:
  name: gke-demo
  namespace: stacks
spec:
  name: gke-demo
  type: TERRAFORM
  approval: true
  detach: false
  manageState: true
  actor: console@plural.sh
  configuration:
    version: 1.8.2
  repositoryRef:
    name: fleet
    namespace: fleets
  clusterRef:
    name: mgmt
    namespace: infra
  workdir: gke-cluster
  git:
    ref: main
    folder: terraform
  files:
  - mountPath: /plural
    secretRef:
      name: gcp-creds
  environment:
  - name: GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS
    value: /plural/creds.json
  - name: TF_VAR_cluster
    value: gke-demo
  - name: TF_VAR_tier
    value: dev
  - name: TF_VAR_fleet
    value: gke-dem
The meaning of this yaml is pretty self-documenting, we are:

creating a TERRAFORM stack, so it will execute the standard terraform workflow
we're using Plural as the state store, removing the need to configure S3 or other backends manually
approval will be required before terraform apply will trigger, ensuring a human verifies the plan first to reduce misconfiguration risk
we're sourcing manifests from the fleet repository (referencing a GitRepository crd)
we're executing on the mgmt cluster (referencing a Cluster crd)
and we're executing in the terraform/gke-cluster folder
You can also see you can bind files and environment variables into the environment, although it is still best practice to use IRSA, GKE workload identity or similar mechanisms for issuing cloud credentials.

issues.title: Shader Translation: Complete translation between Standard Surface to gltf_pbr
issues.body:
In this Issue I have gather all missing inputs we should be able to add in the [standard_surface_to_gltf_pbr.mtlx
](https://github.com/AcademySoftwareFoundation/MaterialX/blob/main/libraries/bxdf/translation/standard_surface_to_gltf_pbr.mtlx) translation graph.

Each topic will have links to both the gltf spec/docs and standard surface docs, and the corresponding inputs for each shading model

Currently these inputs is missing:
- [ ] Alpha
- [ ] Normal, Tangent
- [ ] Specular 
- [ ] Index of Refraction
- [ ] Iridescence
- [ ] Emissive
- [ ] Dispersion

### Alpha
**glTF docs:** [Metallic-Roughness Material](https://registry.khronos.org/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html#metallic-roughness-material) (in the docs alpha is the forth component of base color)
**Standard surface doc:** [3.3 Transparency](https://autodesk.github.io/standard-surface/#closures/transparency)
**gltf_pbr inputs:** `alpha` 
**standard surface inputs:** `opacity`

### Normal, Tangent
**gltf_pbr inputs:** ` normal`, `tangent`
**standard surface inputs:** `normal`, `tangent`
existing issue: [Shader Translation: std surface to gltf_pbr does not handle normal input](https://github.com/AcademySoftwareFoundation/MaterialX/issues/1592)

### Specular 
**gltf extension:** [KHR_materials_specular](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHR_materials_specular/README.md)
**Standard surface docs:** [3.7 Specular reflection](https://autodesk.github.io/standard-surface/#closures/specularreflection)
**gltf_pbr inputs:** `specular` `specular_color`
**standard surface inputs:** `specular`, `specular_color`

### Index of Refraction
**gltf extension:** [KHR_materials_ior](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHR_materials_ior/README.md)
**Standard surface docs:** [3.8 Specular transmission](https://autodesk.github.io/standard-surface/#closures/specularreflection)
**gltf_pbr inputs:** `ior`
**standard surface inputs:** `specular_ior`

### Iridescence
**gltf extension:** [KHR_materials_iridescence](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHR_materials_iridescence/README.md)
**Standard surface docs:** [3.6 Metal 
](https://autodesk.github.io/standard-surface/#closures/metal)
**gltf_pbr inputs:** ` iridescence`, `iridescence_ior`, `iridescence_thickness`
**standard surface inputs:** `thin_film_thickness`, `thin_film_IOR`

Both models use **Belcour and Barla** [Belcour2017](https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3072959.3073620) to model iridescence, should be straight forward.

### Emissive
gltf spec: [Metallic-Roughness Material](https://registry.khronos.org/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html#metallic-roughness-material)
gltf extension: [KHR_materials_emissive_strength](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/tree/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHR_materials_emissive_strength)
Standard Surface docs: [3.5 Emission](https://autodesk.github.io/standard-surface/#closures/emission)
**gltf_pbr inputs:** ` emissive`, `emissive_strength`
**standard surface inputs:** `emission`, `emission_color`

### Attenuation
**gltf extension:** [KHR_materials_volume](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/tree/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHR_materials_volume)
**Standard surface docs:** [3.8 Specular transmission](https://autodesk.github.io/standard-surface/#closures/specularreflection)
**gltf_pbr inputs:** `attenuation_distance`
**standard surface inputs:** `transmission_depth`

### Dispersion
**gltf extension:** [KHR_materials_dispersion](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/tree/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHR_materials_dispersion)
**Standard surface docs:** [3.8 Specular transmission](https://autodesk.github.io/standard-surface/#closures/specularreflection)
**gltf_pbr inputs:** Not implemented - Issue: [Update glTF PBR implementation to support current Khronos definition](https://github.com/AcademySoftwareFoundation/MaterialX/issues/2111)
**standard surface inputs:** `transmission_dispersion`

issues.title: Expand to ``use-implicit-booleaness-not-len`` to catch `len(iterable) == 0` and `>0`
issues.body:
### Current problem

[C1802](https://pylint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/messages/convention/use-implicit-booleaness-not-len.html) currently catches this

Examples 1&2 (currently caught by rule C1802)
```py
fruits = ["orange", "apple"]
vegetables = []

if len(fruits):
    print(fruits)

if not len(vegetables):
    print(vegetables)
```

I come across the following sometimes as well (potentially in botched attempt to fix the the flagged violation above), which I think should be equally flagged as a violation.

Examples 3&4 (not caught by PLC1802)
```py
fruits = ["orange", "apple"]
vegetables = []

if len(fruits) > 0:
    print(fruits)

if len(vegetables) == 0:
    print(vegetables)
```


Examples 5&6 (recommended formulation)
```py
fruits = ["orange", "apple"]
vegetables = []

if fruits:
    print(fruits)

if not vegetables:
    print(vegetables)
```

### Desired solution

Examples 3&4 to be flagged as well

### Additional context

See our previous [discussion](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/16798#issuecomment-2729812152) on this issue.

issues.title: Review and Improve Function Signatures and Docstrings
issues.body:
## Task
Review all functions in the codebase to ensure each has a clear, well-defined signature and a comprehensive docstring. Each docstring should explain the function's purpose, expected input parameters (with types), return values (with types), and any important side effects or exceptions.

### What are Function Signatures?
A function signature is the part of the function definition that specifies the function's name, its parameters (including their names and types), and the return type. A clear signature helps users and developers understand how to call the function and what to expect.

**Example:**
```python
def add_numbers(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Add two integers and return the result."""
```

### What are Docstrings?
A docstring is a special string literal that appears right after the function definition. It documents the function's purpose, describes its parameters and return values, and provides any additional context or usage notes. Good docstrings improve code readability and maintainability.

**Example:**
```python
def add_numbers(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """
    Add two integers.

    Args:
        a (int): The first integer.
        b (int): The second integer.

    Returns:
        int: The sum of a and b.
    """
```

### AI Prompt for MS Copilot GPT-4.1
```
Start with pdf functions file. Make a list of all of the functions and add this list to the new issue. Make a table that grades the function signatures and the docstrings for each function in the file. 
```

### Acceptance Criteria
- Every function in the codebase has a clear, type-annotated signature.
- Every function has a docstring that explains its purpose, parameters, return values, and any exceptions or side effects.
- Docstrings follow a consistent style (e.g., Google, NumPy, or reStructuredText).

---

## Functions in `pdfcb_03b_pdffunctions.py`

| Function/Class         | Signature Present | Type Annotations | Docstring Present | Docstring Quality |
|-----------------------|-------------------|------------------|-------------------|------------------|
| `PDF.__init__`        | Yes               | Yes              | No                | N/A              |
| `PDF.header`          | Yes               | No               | No                | N/A              |
| `PDF.footer`          | Yes               | No               | No                | N/A              |
| `PDF.get_col_widths`  | Yes               | Partial          | Yes               | Minimal          |
| `PDF.create_table`    | Yes               | Partial          | Yes               | Good             |

### Function List
- `PDF.__init__(self, header_text: str = "Header Text", footer_text: str = "Footer Text", image_path: str = "")`
- `PDF.header(self)`
- `PDF.footer(self)`
- `PDF.get_col_widths(self, cell_width, data, table_data)`
- `PDF.create_table(self, table_data, title='', data_size=10, title_size=12, align_data='L', align_header='L', cell_width='uneven', line_space=2.5)`

### Table: Signature and Docstring Grading
| Function              | Signature (A-F) | Type Annotations (A-F) | Docstring (A-F) |
|-----------------------|-----------------|------------------------|-----------------|
| `__init__`            | A               | A                      | F               |
| `header`              | A               | F                      | F               |
| `footer`              | A               | F                      | F               |
| `get_col_widths`      | A               | C                      | D               |
| `create_table`        | A               | C                      | B               |

**Legend:**
- Signature: A = clear, B = minor issues, C = missing defaults/types, D = unclear, F = missing
- Type Annotations: A = all present, C = some missing, F = none
- Docstring: A = excellent, B = good, C = adequate, D = minimal, F = missing

This table can be used to prioritize improvements for each function.

issues.title: Resolve build warning: `'version' contains an expression but should be a constant`
issues.body:
**What needs to be done?**

A build warning is caused by using a property for the `<version>` tag in `distro/sql-script/pom.xml`:


```
./mvnw install -DskipTests -Dskip.frontend.build=true
```

At the beginning:
```
Warning: 281 [WARNING] 
Warning: 281 [WARNING] Some problems were encountered while building the effective model for org.operaton.bpm.distro:operaton-sql-scripts:jar:7.24.0
Warning: 281 [WARNING] 'version' contains an expression but should be a constant. @ org.operaton.bpm.distro:operaton-sql-scripts:${operaton.dbscheme.current.version}, /home/runner/work/operaton/operaton/distro/sql-script/pom.xml, line 12, column 12
Warning: 281 [WARNING] 
Warning: 281 [WARNING] It is highly recommended to fix these problems because they threaten the stability of your build.
Warning: 281 [WARNING] 
Warning: 281 [WARNING] For this reason, future Maven versions might no longer support building such malformed projects.
Warning: 281 [WARNING] 
```

The property is defined in `database/pom.xml` with current value `7.24.0`. Replace the property with this version in `distro/sql-script/pom.xml`.

The property has to be changed when a new DB schema version is initiated. This happens usually with a release. The script `.devenv/scripts/maintenance/init-database-version.py` does this.

Extend the script that it updates `distro/sql-script/pom.xml` with the new specified DB schema version.

from torch._inductor import config

issues.title: See if we can add OSSL_FUNC_SIGNATURE_digest_sign support for ML-DSA
issues.body:
Unfortunately this is a problem deep into EVP_DigestSign().
openssl req calls: [do_X509_REQ_sign()](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/46c8f2a78e24771466af0f15208214fe9e48920f/apps/lib/apps.c#L2369) which calls [X509_REQ_sign_ctx](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/03a9584499589f14363de758fdfb887cbef84790/crypto/x509/x_all.c#L153) which calls [ASN1_item_sign_ctx](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/03a9584499589f14363de758fdfb887cbef84790/crypto/asn1/a_sign.c#L147) which ultimately calls [EVP_DigestSign](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/03a9584499589f14363de758fdfb887cbef84790/crypto/evp/m_sigver.c#L623) and this function fallbacks to EVP_DigestSignUpdate() + EVP_DigestSignFinal() because we do not have a digest_sign interaface internally.

I do not recall why we didn't add it, it may be due to the fact that technically ML-DSA does not allow what is traditionally a digest_sign API for OpenSSL as you can't select the digest for ML-DSA signatures.

I'll use this investigation to open a bug to see if we can add it safely w/o breaking other assumptions in OpenSSL.

_Originally posted by @simo5 in https://github.com/latchset/pkcs11-provider/discussions/638#discussioncomment-14500646_

issues.title: [Bug] Released CRDs are using the controller-gen development version
issues.body:
### Kyverno Version

1.15.0

### Description

## Issue description

All single CRDs files appearing in the release since `1.13.0` are using a `controller-gen.kubebuilder.io/version: (devel)` tag when it should match the versions we are using (`0.17.3` as I'm writing this issue)


```
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  annotations:
    controller-gen.kubebuilder.io/version: (devel) # <=== THIS
  name: ephemeralreports.reports.kyverno.io
spec:
```

## Possible causes

During the release process we are not uploading the same CRDs files as the ones that are then to the `install.yaml` / helm chart. 

This is the code that upload said files: 

https://github.com/kyverno/kyverno/blob/2d801c563bdca1c879c5e1376c0b9b985d541fa6/.github/workflows/release.yaml#L286

```yaml
- name: Upload CRD manifest
  uses: svenstaro/upload-release-action@81c65b7cd4de9b2570615ce3aad67a41de5b1a13 # 2.11.2
  with:
  # ...
    file: config/crds/**/*.yaml
```

By default `config/crds` are uploaded without the version being updated

## Expected

Each single CRDs files that is uploaded should have a proper version like:

```
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  annotations:
    controller-gen.kubebuilder.io/version: v0.17.3
  name: ephemeralreports.reports.kyverno.io
```

_No response_

Update the recipe on ConanCenter to build/supply the latest version of OpenAssetIO.

~~`cpython` is usually only a build dependency of OpenAssetIO.  It can become a runtime/link dependency in the absence of a compatible system Python environment.  It may not even be a necessary build dependency, if the system Python has development artefacts (e.g. headers).~~

This is especially an issue if there are no pre-built binaries available for one or more of the myriad packages (e.g. because the compiler version in use does not match a compiler version on ConanCenter's CI matrix).  Having to build packages is not only slow, it often fails for various random reasons and takes time to debug and work around.~~

issues.title: [Smithy Framework] - Extend our Smithy Framework to Payment Methods Delete API and its corresponding Request/Response Payloads
issues.body:
## Summary

Extend our Smithy Framework to Payment Methods Delete (/payment_methods/{payment_method_id}) DELETE API, an existing Hyperswitch API and its Request/Response Payloads.

## Type 

Feature

## Context  

### What is the Smithy Framework?

__Smithy__ is an Interface Definition Language (IDL) and set of tools created by Amazon for building APIs and SDKs. Think of it as a way to describe your API's structure, data types, and operations in a language-agnostic format, then automatically generate client SDKs, server stubs, documentation, and validation code for multiple programming languages.

### 1. __Rust-to-Smithy Code Generation Pipeline__

Instead of writing Smithy models manually, you've created a system that automatically generates them from your existing Rust code. This is brilliant because:

- You maintain your source of truth in Rust
- Smithy models are automatically kept in sync
- You can generate SDKs for other languages from your Rust types

### 2. __The Three-Crate Architecture__

__`smithy` crate__: Contains the `#[derive(SmithyModel)]` macro that you annotate your Rust structs/enums with.

__`smithy-core` crate__: Contains the core types and logic for:

- Representing Smithy models in Rust
- Converting Rust types to Smithy shapes
- Generating the actual Smithy IDL files

__`smithy-generator` crate__: A build-time tool that:

- Scans your entire workspace for types with `#[derive(SmithyModel)]`
- Collects all the generated models
- Outputs `.smithy` files

### 3. __How the Attribute System Works__

Your implementation requires the `#[smithy(value_type = "...")]` attribute on each field. This is crucial because:

- __Explicit Type Mapping__: Rust types don't always map 1:1 to Smithy types, so you specify exactly how each field should be represented
- __Field Filtering__: Fields without this attribute are ignored, giving you fine-grained control
- __Validation__: You can add constraints like `pattern`, `range`, `length`, etc.

Example usage from your codebase:

```rust
#[derive(SmithyModel)]
#[smithy(namespace = "com.hyperswitch.smithy.types")]
pub struct CustomerDetails {
    #[smithy(value_type = "String")]
    phone_country_code: String,
    
    #[smithy(value_type = "String")]
    email: String,
    
    #[smithy(value_type = "String", required)]
    id: String,
    
    // This field will be ignored in Smithy generation
    internal_field: HashMap<String, String>,
}
```

### 4. __The Generation Process__

I can see from your workspace that you have 65 structs/enums with `#[derive(SmithyModel)]` across various crates:

1. __Build Time__: The `build.rs` script scans your workspace for `#[derive(SmithyModel)]` annotations
2. __Model Collection__: Each annotated type generates a `SmithyModel` containing shapes, constraints, and metadata
3. __IDL Generation__: The generator creates `.smithy` files in the `smithy/models/` directory
4. __SDK Generation__: These `.smithy` files are then used with standard Smithy tooling to generate client SDKs



## Starter tasks

1. __Add the derive macro__ to your struct:

   ```rust
   #[derive(SmithyModel)]
   pub struct YourStruct {
       // fields here
   }
   ```

2. __Add the namespace attribute__ (choose one approach):

     ```rust
     #[derive(SmithyModel)]
     #[smithy(namespace = "com.hyperswitch.your.namespace")]
     pub struct YourStruct {
     ```

3. __Add `value_type` attributes to each field you want in the Smithy model__:

   ```rust
   #[derive(SmithyModel)]
   #[smithy(namespace = "com.hyperswitch.your.namespace")]
   pub struct YourStruct {
       #[smithy(value_type = "String")]
       pub name: String,
       
       #[smithy(value_type = "i64")]
       pub amount: i64,
       
       #[smithy(value_type = "Option<String>")]
       pub optional_field: Option<String>,
       
       // This field will be IGNORED (no smithy attribute)
       internal_field: HashMap<String, String>,
   }
   ```

4. __Add constraints__ (optional but recommended):

   ```rust
   #[derive(SmithyModel)]
   #[smithy(namespace = "com.hyperswitch.your.namespace")]
   pub struct YourStruct {
       #[smithy(value_type = "String", required)]
       pub id: String,
       
       #[smithy(value_type = "String", pattern = "^[a-zA-Z0-9]+$")]
       pub code: String,
       
       #[smithy(value_type = "i64", range = "1..=1000")]
       pub amount: i64,
       
       #[smithy(value_type = "String", length = "1..=255")]
       pub description: String,
   }
   ```

We are enhancing the Smithy framework by adding support for the Payment Methods Delete API. This means annotating the request and response structs for this API with the Smithy macros so that the generator produces the corresponding .smithy models. This keeps our API definitions consistent, allows SDKs to include payment methods deletion, and brings the Payment Methods Delete flow in line with other APIs like Payments Create.
  

## Implementation hints

Refer to Payments Create API and its corresponding Request/Response Payloads, follow the same logic, how it is implemented for the API calls and how the Request/Response payloads are annotated for those APIs.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All types and nested types present in Request/Response payloads must be annotated appropriately. 
- [ ] Run `cargo build` on the project to ensure that no compilation issue exists. 
- [ ] No change in existing business logic or functionality. 
- [ ] Run `smithy validate` to ensure that the Smithy Models generated from the annotated Rust structs are accurate.

issues.title: BUG: assert_frame_equal(check_dtype=False) fails when comparing two DFs containing pd.NA that only differ in dtype (object vs Int32)
issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
from pandas.testing import assert_frame_equal

df1 = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "x": pd.Series([pd.NA], dtype="Int32"),
    }
)
df2 = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "x": pd.Series([pd.NA], dtype="object"),
    }
)

assert_frame_equal(df1, df2, check_dtype=False) # fails, but should succeed
```

### Issue Description

Output of the above example:

```
AssertionError: DataFrame.iloc[:, 0] (column name="x") are different

DataFrame.iloc[:, 0] (column name="x") values are different (100.0 %)
[index]: [0]
[left]:  [nan]
[right]: [<NA>]
```

When comparing DataFrames containing `pd.NA` using `check_dtype=False`, the test incorrectly fails despite the only difference being the dtype (Int32 vs object).

Note that the values in the dataframe really are the same:

```
print(type(df1["x"][0])) # prints <class 'pandas._libs.missing.NAType'>
print(type(df2["x"][0])) # prints <class 'pandas._libs.missing.NAType'>
```

Related issues:
- https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/18463: Similar but "opposite": here the dataframes contain different values (nan vs None) which are incorrectly treated as equal. In this issue, the dataframes contain equal values which are incorrectly treated as different.

### Expected Behavior

The test should succeed, since the only difference is the dtypes, and `check_dtype=False`.

issues.title: Update Resource Timestamp in UTC
issues.body:
## Short
All timestamps should be normalised to the same timezone

## Proposal
Always update timestamps in UTC

## Ratio
The resource abstractor gives every entry (cluster or node) as timestamp. This timestamp is used to ensure that only relevant resource information is used. This timestamp is currently always applied according to local time, meaning that resource information aggregated in one timezone will be incompatible with resource information aggregated in another.

## Impact
Resource Abstractor, System Manager, Cluster Manager

## Development time
1 day

## Status
Looking for feedback

## Checklist

issues.title: fuzzing: Use `wasm-encoder` rather than generating WAT text and then assembling it in dummy imports
issues.body:
In https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/pull/2497#discussion_r541118846 we added support for generating nested modules, and we generate these modules by concatenating strings of WAT and then passing it to `Module::new` which internally checks for WAT strings and assembles them into Wasm bytes if necessary.

We can make this more efficient, improving the number of test cases we fuzz in a given amount of time, by generating Wasm bytes directly via the [`wasm-encoder`](https://docs.rs/wasm-encoder/0.2.0/wasm_encoder/) crate, rather than generating a WAT string. The `wasm-encoder` crate has builder methods that should make it pretty straightforward to translate the `WatGenerator` into a `WasmGenerator`.

If you want to work on this issue, leave a comment, and let me know whatever questions you have!

Info for getting up and running with contributing: https://docs.wasmtime.dev/contributing.html

issues.title: Hardcoded behaviour in `OmegaConfigLoader` should be configurable
issues.body:
## Description

Hardcoded behaviour to ignore hidden folders: https://github.com/kedro-org/kedro/blob/e8727d3539062de23cb16b0bfd68074ac79a2754/kedro/config/omegaconf_config.py#L336

## Context
We are integrating this with another tool where the behaviour is to output folders with a `.`. Unfortunately the tool does not support changing the behaviour to output yaml files into a non-hidden folder (which I think it should configurable but that's an issue for a separate repo). 

## Possible Implementation
Surface this as an additional kwarg, but defaulted to ignore (as per the current implementation) so no breaking change. 
```
class OmegaConfigLoader(AbstractConfigLoader):
    ...

    def __init__(
        ...
        ignore_hidden: bool = True,
    ):
```

## Possible Alternatives

* Tweak the upstream tool to not output hidden folders. 
* Have the user add additional code to `cp` or `mv` the hidden folder to a non-hidden folder (simple but not clean)


Also, hello! 👋 

cc @mb010

Glossaire : Les pages à créer ### Création du contenu Cette partie-là nécessite que vous soyez habitué un minimum à la récupération du contenu originel, à la mise en page des meta données FR ainsi qu'à la traduction de contenu dans le respect des nommages des éléments comme indiqué dans les [Lignes directrices pour la Contribution](https://github.com/mdn/translated-content/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md). **👋🏻 Pour les débutants :** - Vous sont fournis ici les liens vers la documentation d'origine sur le MDN, utilisez le lien en bas de page « _View the source on GitHub_ » pour retrouver le fichier `index.md` de la page, c'est ce fichier qui est à traduire. - Vous devez placer ce fichier dans son chemin à l'identique de la version `en_US` pour le `fr`. (Exemple : **Origine** `./content/files/en-us/glossary/accessible_name/index.md` -> **Version traduite** `./translated-content/files/fr/glossary/accessible_name/index.md`) - Depuis le GitHub vous pouvez également retrouver la clé de version « hash key » en cliquant sur « History / Historique » et en récupérant l'identifiant de la dernière modification avec le bouton « Copy / Copier », la dernière modification en date est située en haut de la liste (cf. image d'exemple). ![Vision de la liste des changements effectués sur l'entrée de Glossaire "Accessible Name" présentant où copier un commit sur GitHub](https://i.imgur.com/4bLA6hP.png) #### 79 pages - issues.title: FEATURE REQUEST: Enhance Classification Prompt for Stricter DevRel Query Handling
issues.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

- [x] Yes, it is related to a problem

### Describe the feature you'd like

### 🌟 Feature Description

This feature focuses on a critical enhancement of the initial **Classification Prompt**. The goal is to refine the prompt's logic to be much stricter and more precise, ensuring that the DevRel agent is only triggered for queries that are explicitly its responsibility. This involves improving the instructions the LLM uses to decide whether a message requires agent intervention.

Additionally, this task includes a secondary objective to review all other existing prompts (`agent_prompt`, `summarization_prompt`, etc.) for clarity, efficiency, and alignment with the latest system architecture.

### 🔍 Problem Statement

Currently, the classification prompt may be too broad, leading to the DevRel agent responding to general conversations or messages where it's not needed. This can create several issues:

1.  **Unnecessary Invocations**: The agent wastes resources processing irrelevant messages.
2.  **User Annoyance**: An AI assistant that injects itself into every conversation can be perceived as intrusive or unhelpful.
3.  **Lack of Precision**: The agent may misinterpret context and provide answers when it should remain silent, degrading the quality of the user experience.

The core problem is a lack of **strict activation boundaries** for the agent.

### 🎯 Expected Outcome

1.  **Modified Classification Prompt**: The `Classification Prompt` will be rewritten to include new, strict rules. The agent should **only** be activated if one of the following conditions is met:
      * The user **explicitly tags or mentions** the DevRel AI bot (e.g., `@Devr.AI, can you help?`).
      * The user's query is a direct question about the project, community, contribution process, or a technical issue clearly related to the repository (e.g., "How do I set up the development environment?", "I'm getting a build error.").
      * The prompt will explicitly instruct the model to **ignore** general chatter, greetings, and conversations between other users unless the bot is tagged.
2.  **Reduced False Positives**: After implementation, there should be a measurable decrease in the number of times the agent responds to irrelevant conversations.
3.  **Improved Prompt Suite**: A brief review of all other system prompts will be conducted, with minor enhancements made for clarity and conciseness.

### Record

- [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct
- [ ] I want to work on implementing this feature

issues.title: Track scan numbers in MGF files
issues.body:
It is unfortunate that scan numbers in MGF files are not retained by Casanovo.  We should make it possible to keep this information, in addition to the scan index. In the future, DepthCharge is going to be modified to be more flexible with the information it parses from the mass spec data files. When that happens, we can use that functionality to track scan numbers.  However, prior to these changes, we could accomplish this by adding to Casanovo a post-processing step wherein the MGF file is read again. It’s not hard to do---something like the following would work:
```
with open("test.mgf") as mgf_file:
    index_counter = 0 
    index2scan = {}
    for line in mgf_file:
        if line.startswith("SCAN ID"):
            index2scan[index_counter] = line.split("=", 1)[1]
            index_counter += 1
```

`index2scan` would be a dictionary mapping the scan index to the scan id value, again assuming all scans had the `SCAN ID` field.

In practice, we should probably support `SCAN ID`, `SCAN` and `SCANS`, since there is no definitive standard for MGF.

issues.title: Support decrypt flag the same way Agenix does
issues.body:
The original Bash Agenix implementation supports a `-d` flag for just decrypting a secret:
```
-d, --decrypt FILE        decrypts FILE to STDOUT
```
While the `ragenix` implementation does not:
```
error: unexpected argument '-d' found

Usage: agenix [OPTIONS] <--edit <FILE>|--rekey|--schema>

For more information, try '--help'.
```
This makes it incompatible with various scripts that were written with `agenix` in mind.

A workaround is using `-e`/`--edit` flag and supplying the `EDITOR=cat` env variable, but it doesn't fix incompatibility with scripts that use `agenix`.

export { jAIPrompt, formatMessage, model, vectorStore };

export { jAIPrompts, formatMessage, model, vectorStore };

Imports all four core utilities (`jAIPrompt`, `model`, `formatMessage`, `vectorStore`) for real-time AI interactions.

**Should be:**

Imports all four core utilities (`jAIPrompts`, `model`, `formatMessage`, `vectorStore`) for real-time AI interactions.

This is a good first issue because:

- ✅ Improves developer experience
- ✅ Easy to verify completion

The actual code implementation is correct (`jAIPrompts` with an "s"), so only the documentation needs updating to match.

issues.title: Support for CKA_EC_POINT raw byte encoding for CKK_EC too
issues.body:
**Describe the feature**
Extend support of #483 not only for Edwards and Montgomery but for classic EC too.

**Expected behavior**
pkcs11-provider successfully decodes both DER encoded (as mandated by the specification) and raw (ill encoded) public CKK_EC keys.

**Additional context**
We noticed that historically we created CKK_EC keys wrong all the time and SoftHSM2 did not care at all. But since we used libp11 engine that contains [workaround](https://github.com/OpenSC/libp11/blob/8b89cad3641c910dbb521cc7b6170b79c87cee87/src/p11_ec.c#L286) for decoding such ill-formed keys we haven't noticed until now while we migrate to pkcs11-provider. It is now too late to migrate existing keys to the correct format but we can add workaround as libp11 does.

issues.title: Add schemeName support to x-security at the workflow level
issues.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

<!-- A clear and concise description of what the problem is. Ex. I'm always frustrated when [...] -->

Currently, in order to define security at the workflow level using `x-security`, we have to inline the entire security scheme. This leads to duplication when the scheme already exists and is referenced elsewhere in the API description. It makes workflows verbose and harder to maintain.

### Describe the solution you'd like

<!-- A clear and concise description of what you want to happen. -->

Allow `x-security` at workflow level to support a `schemeName` field referencing an existing security scheme (via `$sourceDescriptions`) instead of requiring the full scheme object. Example:

```yaml
sourceDescriptions:
  - name: main
    type: openapi
    url: ../main/openapi.yaml

workflows:
  - workflowId: workflowId
    x-security: 
      - schemeName: $sourceDescriptions.main.UserCookie
        values:
          apiKey: {KEY}
```

### Describe alternatives you've considered

<!-- A clear and concise description of any alternative solutions or features you've considered. -->

The current workaround is to inline the scheme every time:

```yaml
workflows:
  - workflowId: workflowId
    x-security: 
      - scheme:
          type: apiKey
          in: cookie
          name: accessToken
        values:
          apiKey: {KEY}
```

This approach is repetitive and error-prone, especially when the same scheme is reused across multiple workflows.

### Additional context

<!-- Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here. -->

Referencing existing schemes improves maintainability and reduces duplication. A common use case is referencing a shared scheme like:

```yaml
UserCookie:
  $ref: ../common/security/UserCookie.yaml
```

Which is defined as:

```yaml
type: apiKey
in: cookie
name: accessToken
description: Default authentication scheme for interaction between browser and API.
```

### References

- [Choose between schemeName and scheme](https://redocly.com/docs/respect/extensions/x-security#choose-between-schemename-and-scheme)
- [no-x-security-scheme-name-in-workflow](https://redocly.com/docs/cli/rules/respect/no-x-security-scheme-name-in-workflow)
